# Heavy metal contamination in rice

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="rice-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="rice-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="rice-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Rice metal levels depend on growing conditions, grain form and preparation ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]). Water management can trade lower inorganic arsenic for higher cadmium ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]).

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Inorganic arsenic and cadmium are central concerns ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Lead, total mercury and chromium are also measured; chemical species remain separate ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Soil, cultivar and water management influence uptake ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]]). Bran retention, milling and cooking change the rice material being compared ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]).

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Compare the same arsenic species and rice preparation ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Check arsenic and cadmium together when changing origin, irrigation or processing, then verify the delivered lot ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]).

</li>
</ul>
</section>

<a id="direct-answer"></a>
<a id="overview"></a>
<a id="decision-summary"></a>
## Rice overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>

Use this review to compare a rice result with the available occurrence evidence, investigate sourcing differences and select controls to verify. The profile covers inorganic and total arsenic, cadmium, lead, nickel, chromium and mercury where measurements are available ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Grain, cooked rice and derived foods retain their own measurement bases ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>
<a id="which-sourcing-or-production-decisions-deserve-priority-on-the-available-evidence"></a>

The most consequential control decision is often the joint response of arsenic and cadmium: a water regime that lowers one can raise the other, while some field settings show lower arsenic without a statistically detected cadmium increase ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]). The evidence below identifies where that distinction changes a sourcing or processing decision.

<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## Rice identity and scope

<a id="grain-fractions-and-derived-ingredients"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>

This page covers edible brown, white and cooked rice. Brown rice retains the bran and germ; polishing removes outer tissues ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). Flour, bran, syrup, protein ingredients and drinks have separate processing and composition evidence ([[sources/jackson2012-arsenic-organic-foods-brown-rice-syrup]]). Uncooked grain describes a food form; dry weight describes an analytical moisture basis ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]).

<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>

<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

<h3 data-hmi-prose-question="true" id="compare-a-rice-result">How does my laboratory result compare?</h3>

Use published concentrations as context for your laboratory result. Match the measurement and reference below. A reference made from study summaries does not establish a percentile for an individual lot ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

<a id="heavy-metal-contamination-profile"></a>
## Heavy metal contamination profile of rice

<a id="chemical-species-and-measurement-basis"></a>
<a id="arsenic-species-across-market-rice"></a>
<a id="cadmium-and-other-elements"></a>
<a id="mercury-species"></a>
<a id="prepared-food-observations"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-007"></a>
<a id="which-metals-and-chemical-species-have-been-investigated-in-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-008"></a>
<a id="what-concentrations-detection-frequencies-and-variability-were-observed-in-each-defined-sampling-frame"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-009"></a>
<a id="which-analyte-questions-are-unassessed-access-blocked-conflicting-or-searched-without-eligible-evidence"></a>
<a id="arsenic-species-and-occurrence-evidence"></a>
<a id="sampling-censoring-and-shared-observations"></a>
<a id="mercury-species-and-comparison-boundaries"></a>

Compare source-reported findings across rice types, collection regions and periods. Low, Moderate and High show each finding’s position against a scoped HMI baseline; they are concentration comparisons, not safety or certainty grades. Different arsenic species and preparation bases remain separate. Open a result for its reference, methods and limitations, or use the information button beside this heading for the comparison methods and scope.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-rice" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-rice-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

HMI pools compatible evidence across sampling families to calculate fixed rice references. The dry-grain references combine FDA category medians with Carey regional medians for inorganic arsenic and DMA, FDA with Myanmar township medians for total arsenic, and Myanmar with Shi country medians for cadmium ([[sources/fda2013-ias-rice-products-sampling]] [[sources/myatsoe2023-myanmar-rice-metals]] [[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). Native-moisture references combine Saudi and Myanmar grain evidence using the Myanmar study’s measured 6–7% moisture loss ([[sources/myatsoe2023-myanmar-rice-metals]] [[sources/alrashdi2024-rice-ias-cd-pb-hg-saudi-arabia]]). Each family receives equal weight; its subgroups share that weight. These references describe subgroup medians in the evidence library, not the median of all rice sold worldwide. Each row’s reported mean or median is compared with that reference; means are never relabelled as medians. Cooked rice remains separate. Low is below Q1, Moderate is Q1–Q3, and High is above Q3; reporting bounds must support one position. The sidebar shows contributing families, conversions, count-weighted and leave-one-family-out sensitivity, and the limitations of single-family references. These are concentration positions, not safety or certainty grades.

<p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Arsenic species and occurrence evidence</p>

Rice occurrence studies cover different chemical species, grain forms and sampling frames ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). The table brings international surveys, field-grown grain, commercial rice products and FDA cooked-rice composites together by analyte, while retaining each source’s reported statistic and measurement basis. A mean, median and detected range answer different questions; the table labels each explicitly.

EFSA’s 2024 organoarsenic assessment adds a separate evidence stream. Its occurrence analysis includes DMA measurements in polished and brown grain, while some processed-food estimates are derived using recipes and an assumption of no processing loss ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]). Direct grain observations and model-derived flour, porridge or beverage values must remain distinguishable ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]). Organic arsenic is not one interchangeable substance with one toxicological interpretation ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]).

<p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Sampling, censoring and shared observations</p>

Sampling and censoring matter as much as the reported concentration. The global cadmium compilation reuses earlier studies and substitutes half the detection limit for low results ([[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). The Henan monitoring summaries also include substituted non-detects ([[sources/yan2025-rice-heavy-metals-henan-china]]). Their reported medians remain usable source summaries, but they are not medians of detected samples and cannot supply a matched trend against the FDA composites ([[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/yan2025-rice-heavy-metals-henan-china]]).

Source rows preserve the counted unit. The Vietnamese field study covers genotypes with paired brown and white grain; the Ethiopian study combines farmers’ grain into area composites ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/desalew2023-rice-ethiopia]]). Multiple analyte rows reuse those same materials ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/desalew2023-rice-ethiopia]]). Neither more rows nor technical repeats create additional independent studies ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/desalew2023-rice-ethiopia]]).

<p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Mercury species and comparison boundaries</p>

Direct mercury measurements remain separate from model outputs. Brombach’s European survey reports both total mercury and methylmercury in a mixture of grain and rice products; its overall range cannot be assigned to a grain-only or baby-food subgroup ([[sources/brombach2017-methylmercury-european-commercial-rice]]). Cui’s spatial model addresses a different question and does not contribute a new measured product distribution to this table ([[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]).

Original source means, medians, ranges and measurement bases remain visible. Recovered individual measurements and regional summaries supply compatible HMI references; the baseline does not require every study to report a percentile. Unknown moisture bases and unresolved reporting limits remain explicit ([[sources/desalew2023-rice-ethiopia]]). Neither below-LOQ results nor an absence of detections establishes zero contamination ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]] [[sources/desalew2023-rice-ethiopia]]).

class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:rice-cooked-tAs:51ea4b31f834"><summary>HMI cooked-rice tAs reference · 4 sampling families</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:rice-cooked-tAs:51ea4b31f834"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI cooked-rice tAs reference · 4 sampling families. Cooked rice as prepared, µg/kg as eaten. Distribution of sample or subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>36</td><td>41.5</td><td>63</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>36</td><td>41.5</td><td>63</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>82 reference units; 4 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FDA Total Diet Study, FY2018–FY2020</td><td>54</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>25</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Authors 2026</td><td>2</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Baxter et al. 2015</td><td>1</td><td>25%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians from every compatible rice sampling family in the evidence ledger for this analyte, material and basis: published subgroup medians, medians HMI calculates from printed per-sample values, FDA Total Diet Study cooked composites and WHO GEMS/Food region-by-year medians (random sampling only). Each family has equal total weight; subgroups have equal weight within a family. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Dry-weight, native-moisture and cooked results are kept in separate references; no moisture conversion is assumed.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>An evidence-library reference, not a probability sample of the world rice market. Sampling families differ in frame (retail, farm, contaminated sites, monitoring) and period; GEMS/Food regions are reporting regions, not growing origins. Many submissions are non-detects with differing limits, which widens the bounds. no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (27)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2018 / CY2017</td><td>Mid-Atlantic / Winter</td><td>5.6</td><td>CSV source row 8332; no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (27)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2018 / CY2017</td><td>Mid-Atlantic / Winter</td><td>&lt;4</td><td>CSV source row 56192; no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (27)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2018 / CY2017</td><td>Mid-Atlantic / Winter</td><td>&lt;1</td><td>CSV source row 8334; no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (27)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2018 / CY2017</td><td>Mid-Atlantic / Winter</td><td>&lt;1</td><td>CSV source row 56193; no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (1)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2019 / CY2019</td><td>Southwest / Summer</td><td>41.6</td><td>CSV source row 8759; fda-tds-ab5e4b731bf63f5cfaea</td></tr></tbody></table></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Original source and locator</summary><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-results">Open the FDA primary source</a> · <a href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020" class="internal" data-slug="sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">HMI source record</a></p><p>summary food 50; iAs; source summary spreadsheet row .</p></details></div><div data-evidence-content><p class="hmi-dataset-title"><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">WHO GEMS/Food</a></p><p>Cooked rice, form not stated · Inorganic arsenic (iAs) · 70 GEMS/Food submissions.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Selected finding and reference</p><div class="hmi-selected-result" data-selected-finding><strong class="hmi-finding">22.9 µg/kg (median)</strong><span class="hmi-row-note">Median.</span><p>70 GEMS/Food submissions. no moisture/basis conversion.</p><div data-shared-evidence-content><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>How the comparison is calculated</summary><p>Earlier matched collections uses the latest selected year and the earliest earlier year with common region × season groups. We calculate a median within each group, then the median across the same groups in each year, with equal group weight. Unmatched composites remain in the source tables. Other collection regions matches fiscal year and season and balances the peer regions. These are descriptive sample comparisons.</p><p>A reference middle 50% is the earlier groups' Q1–Q3, with linear interpolation. It describes that reference set; it is not a normal range, a safety threshold or an outlier test. A single earlier measurement has no meaningful reference distribution.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Sampling, analytical methods and reporting limits</summary><p>Regional results are prepared-food composites from collection markets, not growing origins or individual brands. Fiscal-year coverage is uneven. Matched comparisons retain common region/season strata, with equal stratum weight. Different sampled composites are not a longitudinal panel or a demonstrated population trend.</p><p>FDA regional foods combine purchases from three cities into one prepared-food composite. Row-specific administrative reporting limits are preserved. A non-detect is bounded by its reporting limit; no concentration is imputed. The multi-analyte rice records contain winter-only FY2020 collections; this does not mean every analyte was tested in that year. Matching also addresses unequal regional coverage, including the absence of West in the FY2018 winter subset.</p><p><a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-total-diet-study-tds/fda-total-diet-study-tds-design-and-implementation">FDA collection and preparation design</a> · <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/159746/download?attachment=">Original data key</a></p><p>Unmatched source-year summaries describe every reported sample in that year. The selected comparison uses only its declared matching groups. Different fiscal years can include collections from the same calendar year.</p><p>Collection markets do not identify growing or ingredient origin. Other collection regions compares samples matched by year and season.</p><p>Source-value tables retain public category-level sample identifiers, fiscal year, reported result and original locator. A zero lower interval endpoint is never displayed as an observed concentration.</p></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source reuse limits</summary><p>Comparisons concern the selected historical dataset and are not current supplier rankings, compliance findings or independent measurements. They are descriptive sample comparisons and do not establish a population trend.</p></details></div><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Source values and extraction locators (27)</summary><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Fiscal / calendar year</th><th scope="col">Region / season</th><th scope="col">Reported result (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Source locator</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>FY2018 / CY2017</td><td>Mid-Atlantic / Winter</td><td>&lt;1</td><td>CSV source row 8337; ## Sources and contamination pathways

<a id="soil-water-redox-and-grain-uptake"></a>
<a id="microbial-and-plant-mechanisms"></a>
<a id="does-a-high-soil-concentration-predict-the-grain-concentration"></a>
<a id="what-do-microbial-studies-establish-about-rice-contamination"></a>
<a id="what-do-plant-binding-and-transporter-experiments-establish"></a>
<a id="how-can-the-source-of-contamination-be-traced"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Rice contamination depends on both the metals present in the growing environment and the conditions that make them available to the plant ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). Soil chemistry and water management help explain why grain concentrations do not simply track total soil concentrations ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). Changes in flooding can alter arsenic and cadmium in different directions, so an improvement for one contaminant does not establish an improvement for the other ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]).

Biological processes add another layer of variation. Microbial activity can change arsenic species around the roots, while binding and transport within plants influence uptake and retention ([[sources/dai2025-rice-arsenic-methylation-demethylation-global]] [[sources/mishra2017-rice-arsenic-thiol-complexation]] [[sources/inoue-2024-rice-nramp5-cadmium]]). The evidence connects these processes with differences in contamination, but a microbial association or laboratory mechanism does not by itself establish a treatment that will reliably reduce contaminants in harvested grain ([[sources/dai2025-rice-arsenic-methylation-demethylation-global]] [[sources/cheng2023-cadmium-rice-cultivars-root-microbiome]] [[sources/mishra2017-rice-arsenic-thiol-complexation]] [[sources/inoue-2024-rice-nramp5-cadmium]]).

These findings make source attribution a separate task from measuring the food. A grain result establishes the concentration in the tested material; it does not identify the responsible field process or distinguish among possible inputs ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]] [[sources/tian2021-magnetic-purification-cadmium-lead-grain]]). Investigating a source requires evidence linking the growing environment to the crop, with the sampling conditions and alternative explanations retained ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]). This distinction matters when deciding which control to investigate and what its effects would need to demonstrate.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-can-contamination-be-traced-from-soil-and-water-to-rice-grain" data-anchor="how-can-contamination-be-traced-from-soil-and-water-to-rice-grain" data-question="How can contamination be traced from soil and water to rice grain?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How can contamination be traced from soil and water to rice grain?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The pathway is not simply “more soil metal means proportionally more grain metal.” Mineral binding, pH, redox, microbial transformations and plant transport affect availability ([[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]). A soil screening result identifies an environmental question; a grain measurement answers the food-composition question ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]). Market observations alone cannot identify whether a particular lot’s metal came from geology, irrigation, fertilizer or atmospheric deposition ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]).

A contaminated grain or retail sample does not identify where the metal entered the crop ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]). Testing a proposed pathway needs measurements along that route, such as irrigation water, soil, plant and grain, while considering other inputs and collection timing ([[sources/cui2022-mercury-speciation-rice-china]]). Purifying an analytical extract improves measurement; it does not demonstrate decontamination of the food ([[sources/tian2021-magnetic-purification-cadmium-lead-grain]]).

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-reducing-flooding-always-increase-grain-cadmium" data-anchor="does-reducing-flooding-always-increase-grain-cadmium" data-question="Does reducing flooding always increase grain cadmium?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does reducing flooding always increase grain cadmium?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Flooding changes the soil chemistry that controls plant exposure ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). Reducing conditions can dissolve iron phases that retain arsenic and favor more mobile arsenic species in porewater ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). Drying can increase cadmium availability, so water-management changes need to be evaluated for both analytes ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). The response varies across growing conditions ([[sources/seyfferth2025-rice-water-management-as-hg-cd]] [[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]]). In the Arkansas production-field study, multiple aerations were associated with a 31% lower median grain inorganic arsenic than conventional flooding, while cadmium did not show a statistically significant water-management effect ([[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]). This observational comparison is a regional counterexample to an inevitable cadmium increase ([[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]). It does not establish equivalence or a universal reduction factor ([[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]). The paper’s field-year denominator differs between Methods and Table 1; its summary concentrations remain outside the comparison tables pending reconciliation ([[sources/limmer2026-arkansas-rice-water-management]]).

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-do-microbial-and-plant-transport-studies-establish" data-anchor="what-do-microbial-and-plant-transport-studies-establish" data-question="What do microbial and plant-transport studies establish?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What do microbial and plant-transport studies establish?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Dai and colleagues combine field observations, soil chronosequences, incubations and a global metagenomic survey to examine the balance between arsenic methylation and demethylation, linking microbial functions with grain speciation and straighthead disease ([[sources/dai2025-rice-arsenic-methylation-demethylation-global]]). A larger methylated fraction is not automatically nutritionally preferable ([[sources/dai2025-rice-arsenic-methylation-demethylation-global]]). Cheng and colleagues compare two rice cultivars and their root-associated microbiomes under soil amendments ([[sources/cheng2023-cadmium-rice-cultivars-root-microbiome]]). The lower-accumulating cultivar also had distinctive microbial and soil features ([[sources/cheng2023-cadmium-rice-cultivars-root-microbiome]]). Such coupled findings make biological mechanisms plausible, but a microbial association or predictive model is not by itself proof that adding one organism will lower harvested-grain cadmium under another field’s conditions ([[sources/cheng2023-cadmium-rice-cultivars-root-microbiome]]).

Mishra’s arsenic work examines species transformation and thiol binding in exposed rice plants ([[sources/mishra2017-rice-arsenic-thiol-complexation]]). Inoue’s Nramp5 engineering study uses a yeast assay to examine cadmium and manganese uptake selectivity ([[sources/inoue-2024-rice-nramp5-cadmium]]). These studies help explain transport and retention; their experimental systems do not provide a market-rice concentration distribution or a demonstrated reduction in dietary exposure ([[sources/mishra2017-rice-arsenic-thiol-complexation]] [[sources/inoue-2024-rice-nramp5-cadmium]]).

</div>
</details>



<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Variation by origin, variety and growing conditions

<a id="rice-sourcing-differences"></a>
<a id="origin-and-sourcing"></a>
<a id="cultivar-and-growing-conditions"></a>
<a id="collection-year"></a>
<a id="what-does-the-climate-experiment-tell-us-about-future-crops"></a>
<a id="what-can-climate-experiments-tell-us-about-future-crops"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

Rice contamination varies both between and within sampled growing regions, so an origin label provides context rather than a concentration for every supplier or lot ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). Geographic comparisons also depend on what was sampled: a growing location and a retail collection market describe different parts of the supply chain ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Useful comparisons retain the rice form, measurement basis and sampling scope alongside the location ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]] [[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

The surveys identify useful lower-contamination candidates: Carey’s polished-rice survey reported the lowest inorganic-arsenic median in Malawi, 5 µg/kg (19 samples), followed by Tanzania, 9 µg/kg (88 samples), on freeze-dried grain ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]]). Shi’s cadmium survey placed both countries among the lowest reported medians at 4.9 µg/kg, but that number substitutes half the 9.8 µg/kg detection limit rather than measuring an exact low concentration ([[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). These historical market samples suggest origins to investigate for both analytes; they do not guarantee current lots or establish the lowest source for nickel, lead or mercury.

Variety and growing conditions need to be considered together ([[sources/liu2020-rice-gwas-ionomics]]). A low result in one setting does not establish stable performance across soils, water regimes and seasons; climate and soil-arsenic experiments likewise describe responses under particular tested conditions ([[sources/liu2020-rice-gwas-ionomics]] [[sources/muehe2019-rice-climate-arsenic]]). These findings support evaluating a variety in the conditions where it will be grown, without turning a greenhouse result into a universal forecast for future crops ([[sources/liu2020-rice-gwas-ionomics]] [[sources/muehe2019-rice-climate-arsenic]]).

Collection-year differences need similar care because the sampled foods and collection coverage can change ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Matched historical comparisons can describe differences within the available samples, but they do not automatically establish a national trend or a change at a particular supplier ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). For a sourcing decision, the survey evidence provides context for investigating harvest and lot histories rather than replacing measurements of the material being purchased ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-can-growing-origin-tell-us-about-contamination" data-anchor="how-much-can-growing-origin-tell-us-about-contamination" data-question="How much can growing origin tell us about contamination?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much can growing origin tell us about contamination?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Origin helps identify sourcing options to investigate ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). International rice surveys show variation between and within sampled countries, but cultivar, milling, water management and harvest conditions also contribute ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/shi2020-rice-grain-cadmium-global-supply-chain]]). Confirm whether a location means growing origin or collection market: FDA collection regions describe where foods were purchased, not where the rice was grown ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-a-low-accumulating-variety-remain-low-under-different-growing-conditions" data-anchor="does-a-low-accumulating-variety-remain-low-under-different-growing-conditions" data-question="Does a low-accumulating variety remain low under different growing conditions?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does a low-accumulating variety remain low under different growing conditions?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Select a cultivar for the conditions in which it will be grown. Liu’s contrasting-environment study and Tran’s paired brown/white grain study show that genetic and grain-fraction differences matter, but a low result in one setting does not establish stable performance across soils, irrigation regimes and seasons ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/liu2020-rice-gwas-ionomics]]). A useful supplier comparison retains these conditions alongside grain measurements.

Muehe’s greenhouse experiment examines climate and soil arsenic together and finds that their combined effects can alter rice yield and grain arsenic ([[sources/muehe2019-rice-climate-arsenic]]). It is a treatment-specific experiment, not a prediction that every future crop will show the same percentage change ([[sources/muehe2019-rice-climate-arsenic]]). It strengthens the case for testing cultivar performance under the growing conditions in which it will actually be used.

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="do-differences-between-collection-years-demonstrate-a-trend" data-anchor="do-differences-between-collection-years-demonstrate-a-trend" data-question="Do differences between collection years demonstrate a trend?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Do differences between collection years demonstrate a trend?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Collection year can matter when growing conditions, sourcing or processing change. Compare periods with a compatible sampling design. In five shared winter-region groups, FDA cooked white-rice cadmium medians changed from 4.3 to 5.0 µg/kg and brown-rice medians from 5.5 to 9.8 µg/kg between FY2018 and FY2020 ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). The comparison uses six earlier and five later composites; it describes these matched samples, not a national trend ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]). Use the year and region controls to inspect the available matched comparisons. For a purchasing decision, request the supplier’s own harvest and lot history as well: a change in historical survey samples does not identify a change at that supplier ([[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020]]).

</div>
</details>


<a id="processing-effects"></a>
<a id="ingredient-derivative-risk"></a>
## Processing effects and derivatives

<a id="milling-and-fractionation"></a>
<a id="cooking-soaking-and-water-quality"></a>
<a id="are-chemical-soaking-studies-equivalent-to-ordinary-rinsing"></a>
<a id="syrup-protein-flour-and-drinks"></a>
<a id="what-would-demonstrate-actual-metal-removal-rather-than-dilution"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Processing changes which rice material is consumed and how its contaminant concentration should be interpreted ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). Polishing can lower arsenic and many other elements, but the paired brown-and-white grain evidence does not support a universal cadmium reduction ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). The retained grain and removed fractions therefore need their own interpretation, especially when both enter the food or feed chain ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]).

Cooking and pretreatment effects depend on the chemical species, water conditions and process used ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/pogoson2020-rice-cooking-cadmium-arsenic]]). Some tested methods lower residual inorganic arsenic, while rinsing alone has limited benefit and nutrient losses can accompany treatment ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]). Experimental chemical soaking differs from ordinary household rinsing; neither its results nor a cooking-study percentage supplies a universal reduction factor ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/pogoson2020-rice-cooking-cadmium-arsenic]]).

A lower concentration in a rice-derived ingredient does not by itself demonstrate removal of contaminant mass ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]). Milling can redistribute contaminants, water can dilute a product, and changes in chemical species can affect interpretation ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]] [[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]). Verification needs measurements in the final material alongside moisture, yield and outgoing streams, rather than a general conversion from grain results or an assumption that processing leaves every species unchanged ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]] [[sources/hosojima2017-rice-endosperm-protein-cadmium]] [[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]).

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-does-milling-change-contamination-in-rice-and-its-fractions" data-anchor="how-does-milling-change-contamination-in-rice-and-its-fractions" data-question="How does milling change contamination in rice and its fractions?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How does milling change contamination in rice and its fractions?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Polishing can lower arsenic and many other elements, but it is not a reliable universal cadmium control ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). Tran’s study measured brown and white grain from the same plants: most measured elements were higher in brown grain, while cadmium and molybdenum were exceptions ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). That paired design is more informative about milling than comparing unrelated retail products ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). Test the retained grain and the removed bran if both enter the food or feed chain.

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-cooking-and-other-treatments-affect-contaminant-levels" data-anchor="how-do-cooking-and-other-treatments-affect-contaminant-levels" data-question="How do cooking and other treatments affect contaminant levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do cooking and other treatments affect contaminant levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Rinsing alone has limited arsenic benefit; FDA guidance also notes possible nutrient losses from rinsing or excess-water cooking of enriched rice ([[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]). Cooking methods need their own evidence. Carey’s cooking experiments distinguish excess-water cooking from percolation ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]). At a 12:1 water:rice ratio, the study reports 57 ± 5% lower residual-grain inorganic arsenic across the tested materials; the meaning of the reported uncertainty term remains unresolved here ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]). That result concerns the tested method and endpoint, not a common reduction factor for cadmium, methylmercury or all household cooking ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]).

Pogoson’s process is substantially different: sequential chemical soaks, each lasting 12 hours, followed by cooking ([[sources/pogoson2020-rice-cooking-cadmium-arsenic]]). The primary manuscript reports reductions in Cd, inorganic As and DMA, but the starting-species quantities in the stored extraction need arm and basis reconciliation ([[sources/pogoson2020-rice-cooking-cadmium-arsenic]]). The process belongs in the evidence on potential preprocessing; it should not be presented as ordinary rinsing or a validated household instruction ([[sources/pogoson2020-rice-cooking-cadmium-arsenic]]).

Removal into discarded water differs from dilution by water retained in cooked food ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]). A process comparison should retain the starting and residual food concentration, food yield, water quality, drainage and waste destination. FDA guidance also notes that some excess-water methods reduce nutrients ([[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]). Reusing contaminated water or ignoring the discarded stream can change the exposure or environmental consequence ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]).

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="do-lower-concentrations-in-rice-derived-ingredients-demonstrate-metal-removal" data-anchor="do-lower-concentrations-in-rice-derived-ingredients-demonstrate-metal-removal" data-question="Do lower concentrations in rice-derived ingredients demonstrate metal removal?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Do lower concentrations in rice-derived ingredients demonstrate metal removal?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Derivative evidence confirms the need to measure the final material. Hosojima’s protein-powder study includes a contaminant composition table, while Zhao tests microbial immobilization to remove cadmium from contaminated rice flour ([[sources/hosojima2017-rice-endosperm-protein-cadmium]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]). One describes a specific ingredient used in a nutrition trial; the other evaluates a processing method ([[sources/hosojima2017-rice-endosperm-protein-cadmium]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]). Neither supplies a universal grain-to-protein or grain-to-flour conversion, and laboratory removal requires separate process-safety and residual-food validation ([[sources/hosojima2017-rice-endosperm-protein-cadmium]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]).

Jackson’s rice-syrup-containing foods and D’Amato’s Italian-market beverages show why formulation and material identity travel with the result ([[sources/jackson2012-arsenic-organic-foods-brown-rice-syrup]] [[sources/damato2026-inorganic-arsenic-rice-based-beverages]]). The beverage study separately measures arsenic species, rather than estimating inorganic arsenic from a generic total-arsenic fraction ([[sources/damato2026-inorganic-arsenic-rice-based-beverages]]). Its liquid-food concentrations cannot be compared directly with dry grain without accounting for rice inclusion and water ([[sources/damato2026-inorganic-arsenic-rice-based-beverages]]). The [[regulations/eu2023-arsenic-rice-based-drinks|rice-based-drink regulatory scope]] is a distinct category with a selected EU provision shown in the requirements table ([[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels]]).

EFSA’s organoarsenic assessment describes thiolated species and evidence of transformation during processing, storage and acidic extraction ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]). Its processed-commodity scenarios partly assume no DMA loss ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]). These models cannot establish what actually happens in a particular puffed, stored or hydrolysed product ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]). Species-preserving measurements and the relevant original processing studies are needed to resolve that question ([[sources/efsa2024-organoarsenic-species]]).

A useful process calculation measures metal mass in the incoming rice and in each outgoing food, bran, water or sorbent stream, alongside moisture and yield ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]). A lower concentration in a wetter product can occur without the same reduction in total metal mass ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]). A process that transfers metal to waste also requires a disposal assessment; testing only the final concentration leaves that question unanswered ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/zhao2021-cadmium-removal-rice-flour]]).

</div>
</details>



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Heavy metal mitigation and remediation for rice

<a id="agronomic-controls"></a>
<a id="selection-processing-and-formulation"></a>
<a id="consumer-preparation"></a>
<a id="agronomic-levers"></a>
<a id="manufacturing-levers-and-controls"></a>
<a id="consumer-controls"></a>
<a id="how-should-two-controls-with-different-percentage-reductions-be-compared"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>

Rice controls act at different stages, and their effects depend on the contaminant, material and growing conditions ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]] [[sources/sun2023-biochar-rice-cadmium-field]]). Field water management can lower grain inorganic arsenic while increasing cadmium, while soil treatments and cultivar selection address other influences on grain accumulation ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]] [[sources/sun2023-biochar-rice-cadmium-field]]). These findings support matching a control to the grain and conditions being evaluated rather than treating a reduction in one metal as a general reduction in contamination ([[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]] [[sources/sun2023-biochar-rice-cadmium-field]]).

<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>

After harvest, source qualification, milling and preparation address different parts of the problem ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]] [[sources/fda2020-ias-infant-rice-cereal-guidance]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]). Polishing changes contaminant concentrations across grain fractions, with responses that differ by element ([[sources/tran2024-arsenic-cadmium-vietnamese-rice-qtl]]). Some cooking methods reduce residual inorganic arsenic, while rinsing alone has limited benefit and nutrient losses can accompany treatment ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]). A preparation result therefore applies to the tested method and food rather than providing a common reduction factor for every process ([[sources/carey2015-rice-arsenic-percolating-cooking]]).

<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Control performance depends on the chemical species, food material, starting condition and endpoint being compared ([[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]] [[sources/sun2023-biochar-rice-cadmium-field]]). A large relative decrease can leave an important residual concentration, so verification needs the remaining concentration, uncertainty, linked contaminant changes, nutrients and operating conditions ([[sources/limmer2024-arsenic-cadmium-rice-irrigation]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]] [[sources/sun2023-biochar-rice-cadmium-field]]). Historical market contrasts and agency recommendations can inform control selection, but they do not establish an experimental treatment effect or demonstrate commercial performance ([[sources/carey2020-global-low-ias-rice-sourcing]] [[sources/fda-arsenic-exposure-consumer-guidance]]).

Direction is shown separately. These are descriptive display bands, not validated efficacy cutoffs, occurrence-baseline positions, statistical significance, evidence certainty, safety or net benefit. A range spanning bands retains both labels; a qualitative label has no implied percentage.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Control in context</p><p>Evaluate irrigation against both Cd and iAs before changing farm practice.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Context</th><th scope="col">Selected control</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Material</td><td>polished rice grain; Oryza sativa CLXL745</td></tr><tr><td>Stage</td><td>cultivation</td></tr><tr><td>Audience</td><td>Ingredient suppliers</td></tr><tr><td>Period</td><td>Year 1</td></tr><tr><td>Conditions</td><td>Water at −30 cm water table; no standing flood. Rough-rice yield means were lower; the treatment effect was not statistically significant. Costs remain unextracted.</td></tr><tr><td>Verification</td><td>Harvested-grain Cd and iAs, yield, soil and water records.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Design, applicability and operating conditions</p><p>randomized complete block. CLXL745; Delaware clay-loam Ultisol, pH 5.9. Nonflooded paddies watered at a water table 30 cm below ground, without flooding. All paddies flooded until approximately two weeks after transplanting.</p><p>18 mesocosms, three per regime, repeated over two years; not 36 independent farms</p><p>two growing seasons; calendar years not verified in this pilot</p><p>soil-water chemistry and availability; mean (SD), n=3</td><td>Air-dried grain; analytical moisture correction unspecified.</td><td>Supplement Table S5, Year 2, Ripe Grain row, Flood and Nonflood columns; means (SD), n=3.</td></tr><tr><td>Inorganic arsenic (iAs)</td><td>Year 1</td><td>32.0% · HMI-derived</td><td>122 → 83 µg/kg</td><td>0.122 (0.009) → 0.083 (0.007) mg/kg;
